Property Rights

ECON 104 · September 1, 2026

Outline of the Lecture

Property rights shape how we live, exchange, and resolve conflict over scarce resources.

1

What are property rights?

Ownership means the ability to exclude, use, and exchange.

2

Why private property matters

It creates peace, security, and the basis for exchange.

3

Property rights in practice

Real-world problems – and how private property solves them.

ECON 104
02

Property Rights Are About Ownership

ECON 104
03

Property Rights

  • A set of social relationships that define our ability to exercise choices over goods.
  • Property rights give the holder the right to an action, not a right to an object itself.
    • A homeowner may contract out the right to live and reside, but not the right to sell to a tenant.
  • Property rights exist because scarcity necessitates we make choices about how resources are allocated.
ECON 104
04

Limited Resources and How We Allocate Them

  • Imagine two people whose resources have just fallen from heaven – like manna.
  • They now face a tradeoff between production and protection (or predation).
  • You can either spend effort using your resources productively, or you can keep fighting over them.
  • Fighting over scarce resources is unproductive and destructive – you expend other valuable resources (time, energy), but nobody gains anything.
  • It would be better for both individuals to come to an agreement over ownership.
ECON 104
05

This agreement is what we know as property rights.

ECON 104
06

Who Owns Property?

1

Public ownership

A national park.

2

Collective ownership

An HOA pool, or a condo’s common area.

3

Private ownership

Your car, or your laptop.

ECON 104
07

What Is Private Property?

  • The ability to exclude
  • The ability to use
  • The ability to transfer or exchange
ECON 104
08

The Ability to Exclude

  • The ability to exclude other people from accessing your property.
  • But others can also exclude you from accessing their resources.
  • Owners are protected from private and public predation.

A wall makes for good neighbors.

Implication: concentrates both costs and benefits over the use of a resource.
ECON 104
09

What Happens in the Absence of This Ability?

Overconsumption of a Good

An unregulated fishery, or the office fridge that never has anything left in it.

Overproduction of a Bad

A factory dumping waste into a river everyone shares.

ECON 104
10

The Ability to Use

  • The ability to derive benefits from the consumption of a good
    • For present consumption
    • For future consumption
  • This implies the right to cash flows – you have control over any gains or losses that your resources produce.
ECON 104
11

The Ability to Exchange

  • The ability to transfer ownership of a good.
  • This is the distinguishing attribute of private property rights!
  • In collective ownership you can exclude and use, but you cannot transfer!
  • Exchange allows us to allocate a good to its highest valued end.
ECON 104
12

Let’s Think About the Property Rights We Have in the Classroom

  • Can you exclude?
  • Can you use?
  • Can you exchange?
ECON 104
13

Why Should You Care About Private Property Rights?

ECON 104
14

Private Property Creates Conditions of Peace and Security to Make Investments

  • Creates incentives for caring about your resources.
    • If the owner takes care of their resources, they receive the benefits of doing so.
    • If they neglect or waste their resources, they have to bear the costs of doing so.
  • Creates incentives to care about the future.
    • Cash flow rights – the value of your resource is also based on its expected future value.
    • A resource that yields today and tomorrow is more valuable than a resource that yields only today.
ECON 104
15

Private Property Is the Basis of Exchange

1

Productive specialization

2

Productive investment

3

Economic calculation

ECON 104
16

Accountability

  • Owners are incentivized to minimize the damage caused by their property – and to others’ property.
  • This is the very idea of taking “ownership” of something.
ECON 104
17

Private Property Allows for Reconciliation of Conflicting Ends!

  • Two people want the same resource.
  • One person owns it.
  • They can make an offer to the owner, that the owner may accept.
  • Private property allows peaceful transfer of resources!
ECON 104
18

Property Rights Problems in Everyday Life

1

Shared microwaves in a dorm

Here, in the absence of private property rights, the benefits of production and maintenance are dispersed, but the costs are concentrated.
2

The cluttered desk in “The Intern”

3

The office coffee pot nobody refills

ECON 104
19

Drunk Driving as a Property Rights Problem

  • Drunk driving is a proximate cause of accidents on the road.
  • Bad food, bad service, or unclean premises are proximate causes of a restaurant closing down.
  • The actual problem is management.
  • If the management was good, they would have changed these variables.
  • Similarly, if people owned roads and were responsible for providing safety, they would come up with solutions.
  • Private individuals do consider external effects from drunk people – consider bouncers at a club.
ECON 104
20

Property Rights as Solutions

  • Many perceived “public policy” problems are ultimately property rights problems.
  • Smoking in restaurants
  • Cap-and-trade emissions permits
  • Privatizing roads
ECON 104
21

Trade-Offs, Trade-Offs

  • Private property is great, but it comes with transaction costs.
  • Costs of measuring and enforcement.
  • These costs may reduce the bargaining range, but not exhaust it.

Gains from Trade

Production, Specialization, and Exchange

ECON 104
23

Overview of This Lecture

Trade creates value and wealth – in three ways.

1

Different preferences

Trade makes people better off when preferences differ.

2

Specialization

Trade increases productivity through specialization and the division of knowledge.

3

Comparative advantage

Trade increases productivity through comparative advantage.

ECON 104
24

The Double Thank-You Moment

Think about the last time you took an Uber.

  • You probably thanked the driver for the ride – and they probably thanked you for the money.
  • You both benefited from the trade.
Voluntary exchange

Also called a “mutually beneficial exchange” – or, as the professor likes to call it, a “double thank-you moment.”

ECON 104
25

Gains from Trade from Differences in Preferences

Think about the last time you went trick-or-treating on Halloween – did you exchange candy with a friend or sibling afterward?

You exchanged because you expected to be better off – because you and your trading partner have different preferences.
ECON 104
26

Gains from Specialization

  • We don’t just have different preferences – we also have different natural abilities, skills, interests, and access to resources.
  • Trade creates value even if the total number of goods doesn’t change.
  • But trade also creates more goods. How? Specialization.

An Economist Goes to a Pin Factory

A pin factory has eighteen separate tasks – straightening the wire, sharpening the point, attaching the head, and so on.

~20/day
Pins per worker, working alone through all eighteen tasks
48,000/day
Pins per day from ten workers, each specializing in one task
ECON 104
32

Adam Smith’s Benefits of Specialization

1

Dexterity

Greater skill from each worker, learned by doing.

2

No switching time

Workers save the time otherwise lost moving between tasks.

3

Invention & machinery

Specialists are more likely to invent and use better machinery.

This idea is the division of labor. Other benefits include economies of scale and the benefits of specialized knowledge.
ECON 104
33

Limited by the Extent of the Market

“This is awesome! Can we indefinitely keep extending this?” No – the division of labor is limited by the extent of the market.

ECON 104
34

Specialization at a Hospital

  • You don’t just see a “doctor” – you see a specialist.
  • You might see a radiologist for an X-ray, and an anesthesiologist for surgery.
  • And an administrator handles billing and everything else.
  • A hospital runs because so many different specialists work together to produce the outcome.
  • Could you find a pediatric gastroenterologist in the middle of nowhere, Kansas?
ECON 104
35

Absolute Advantage

Absolute advantage

When one producer requires fewer inputs or resources to create a good.

Samrudha has an absolute advantage in samosas; Molly has an absolute advantage in producing brownies.

Comparative Advantage

Comparative advantage

The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer.

ECON 104
45

Comparative Advantage

  • Samrudha has a comparative advantage in samosas.
  • Molly has a comparative advantage in brownies.
  • So Samrudha produces samosas, and Molly makes brownies.
ECON 104
46

Samrudha’s Production Possibilities Frontier

How much can I make with the resources I have?

How many samosas does Samrudha need to give up for each additional brownie?
ECON 104
47

Molly’s Production Possibilities Frontier

How much can Molly produce with what she has?

How many samosas does Molly need to give up for each additional brownie?
